bhakti
(‘devotion’)
------------------------------------------
Bhakti or devotion or love of God is one of the most widely recognised religious sentiments in all the major religions of the world. In हिन्दुइस्म्, its origins can be traced even to the Ṛgveda itself. Praise of God (1.156.3), hearing or recitation of his names as also surrender to him (1.156.2), filial affection towards God (8.98.11), that he seeks his devotees (6.47.17), that he is our dearest and nearest (10.82.3)—these are some of the aspects of भक्ति found in it.
Coming to the उपनिषद्स्, we see that though they are mainly devoted to ज्ञान or knowledge, the doctrine of grace which is an important aspect of the philosophy of devotion, is found in some statements like, ‘Whom the आत्मन् chooses, by him is He obtained; to him, He reveals Himself’. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.23) So also another: ‘When he who is devoid of desire-motivated actions, through the grace of God, the Supporter, sees the परमात्मन्’s glory, then does he become freed from sorrow’ (ibid 2.20). The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad actually uses the word ‘bhakti’ and clearly states ‘prapatti’ (self-surrender) also (6.23; 6.18).
In the Bhagavadgītā, as also in the epics and the purāṅas, भक्ति has been dealt with extensively. In the later literature, treatises specially devoted to delineating the doctrine of भक्ति have also appeared, thus enriching the cult of devotion, like Śāṇḍilya-भक्ति-sūtras, नारद-भक्ति-sūtras, नारद-pāñca-rātra, भक्ति-rasāyana, भक्ति-rasāmṛta-sindhu and so on.
The philosophy of भक्ति, called ‘Bhāgavatadarśana’ accepts God as Personal, though the transcendental aspect too is not taboo. That he can be apprehended neither by the senses nor by the intellect, but only by devotion to him and his grace, is another cardinal principle. That the path of भक्ति is open to all without exception and that is much easier than the other well-known paths like ज्ञान (knowledge) or योग (contemplation), is another doctrine often propagated.
Bhakti has been defined as ‘parama-prema’ (intense love) or ‘parā-anurakti’ (extreme attachment) to God, thus excluding or transcending all other kinds of love. And, this is also ‘parā-भक्ति’ or supreme devotion, which comes as the fulfilment of the practice of devotion. All other practices of devotion that are preliminary, but ultimately lead to parā-भक्ति, are called ‘aparā-भक्ति’.
Categorisation of भक्ति depends upon the standpoint adopted for the purpose. Division according to the guṇas, listing भक्ति as sāttvika, rājasa and tāmasa, is one method; according to the state of मिन्द् of the votary, as भक्ति of the आर्त (the afflicted), of the arthārthi (the one seeking worldly gains), of the jijñāsu (an inquirer of Truth) and of the jñāni (the enlightened one) is another method. A third method depends upon the attitude of the devotee towards God. For instance, śānta is the devotion of a serene votary, dāsya of a servant, sakhya of a friend, vātsalya of a parent and madhura of a consort.
One who aspires after cultivating भक्ति is expected to adopt certain moral and spiritual disciplines in life. Avoiding evil company and cultivating holy company, detachment towards worldly things, taking recourse to lonely places conducive to devotion, giving up evil actions and actions motivated by selfish desires, performing one’s duties as an act of worship of God, practising fortitude and dependence upon God, are some of the disciplines recommended.
The actual act of devotion itself can take several forms such as listening to and singing the glories of God, ritualistic worship, repetition of the divine names and contemplation on the divine forms of God, dedicating the fruits of action to God and an attitude of utter surrender.
Scriptures of भक्ति do not prohibit a person from living an active life in the world. They only advise him to couple God with it. As regards the sins of omission and commission, a sincere repentance and prayer, and the consequent descent of God’s grace, will efface them.
See also धर्म">BHĀGAVATA-DHARMA, BHAKTA and BHAKTIYOGA.

Bhakta-Vighneśvara
(‘Lord of obstacles, dear to the devotees’)
------------------------------------------
Gaṇapati or गणेश, the elephant-faced god of the Hindu pantheon is one of the most popular and widely worshipped deities. He has a very large variety of aspects and भक्त-विघ्नेश्वर, also called भक्त-गणपति, is one of them.
Iconographical works describe him as shining like the autumnal मोओन्. He has four hands in which he carries a coconut, a mango fruit, a lump of sugar and a cup of pāyasa (pudding). In some descriptions a plantain replaces the lump of sugar.
See also GAṆAPATI.

Bhaktiyoga
(‘union with [God] through devotion’)
------------------------------------------
Hindu scriptural works posit मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् from transmigratory existence, as the final goal of life. This can be achieved either through ज्ञान (know-ledge) or through भक्ति (devotion). The well-known path of भक्ति or devotion that ultimately leads to योग or union with, or, being firmly rooted in, God is termed ‘Bhaktiyoga’.
God has been described in the उपनिषद्स् both as the transcendent and as the immanent Spirit (Brahman-आत्मन्), as also a Person with infinite blessed qualities (Aupaniṣada-पुरुष or ईश्वर). In भक्तियोग, the stress is almost entirely on the latter aspect, though the former is accepted.
Dhyāna or meditation on the form of the deity and जप or repetition of the divine name are the chief disciplines of this योग.
Diverse forms of one and the same God, first articulated in the Ṛgveda (1.64.46; 10.114.5), have received a much more detailed treatment in the पुराणस् and allied literature, as a result of the growth of various cults. These have come in very handy for the votaries of the भक्ति cult advocating भक्तियोग. meditation on anyone of the forms of God that one cherishes—and this is called the ‘Iṣṭadevatā’—and repetition of the मन्त्र or the divine name associated with it, has been a popular and effective mode of spiritual practice in भक्तियोग. However, as per the age-old tradition, this मन्त्र has to be received from a qualified गुरु or spiritual preceptor in a ceremonial way, called ‘dīkṣā’.
A person to be qualified as a गुरु has to be sinless, fairly well-versed in the concerned spiritual literature and deeply rooted in God. Anyone who wishes to be a disciple should have cultivated the elementary moral virtues like सत्य or truth and दम or self-control. He should approach the गुरु in all humility and do personal service also. He should receive the मन्त्र with great श्रद्धा or faith and adhere strictly to the instructions given by him.
Apart from जप or repetition of the divine name, other aspects of the practice of भक्तियोग are: śravaṇa (listening to the stories of God), कीर्तन (singing devotional hymns and songs), arcana (ritualistic worship), vandana (obeisance), culti-vation of anyone of the well-known attitudes like dāsya, sakhya or vātsalya and so on.
The saints, sages and seers who have attained perfection by following the path of भक्ति or devotion, are legion. Their characteristics like universal love and compassion, absolute selfcontrol, unselfishness to the core, equanimity under all vicissitudes of life are common to all the perfected beings who might have attained that state by other well-known means of sādhanā like ज्ञान or knowledge.
See also BHAKTA and BHAKTI.

bhakta
(‘devotee’)
------------------------------------------
Bhakti or devotion to God has been recognised as one of the easiest, but most efficacious, method of sādhanā or spiritual practice, ultimately leading to beatitude. One who cultivates such devotion is called a ‘bhakta;’ and, the path of भक्ति itself systematised as a spiritual discipline is named ‘Bhaktiyoga’.
A भक्त or a devotee of God is expected to cultivate certain virtues such as विवेक (discrimination regarding ड़ोओद्), vimoka (freedom from desire), अभ्यास (regular practice of disciplines), kriyā (doing good to others), kalyāṇa (purity through truth, straightforwardness, compassion and non-violence), anavasāda (cheerfulness) and anuddharṣa (absence of hilarity).
Other disciplines he is expected to follow are: viṣayatyāga (renunciation of objects of desire), saṅgatyāga (giving up mental attachment towards them), avyā-vṛtta-भजन (constant and continuous thinking of the Lord), śravaṇa and मनन (hearing about and singing the glories of God), mahatsaṅga (cultivation of holy company), totally abjuring dussaṅga or evil company, taking recourse to viviktasthāna or lonely and peaceful places conducive to the cultivation of भक्ति, complete dependence on God, performance of duties, but dedicating their fruits to God and so on.
The bhaktas can be divided into three groups depending upon the गुण or the nature of their devotion. As is well-known, there are three guṇas—sattva रजस् and तमस्. The sāttvika भक्त practises disciplines of भक्ति to purify himself and to please the Lord. The rājasa भक्त practises devotion to gain worldly benefits. The tāmasa भक्त practises his devotions to bring harm upon others, out of jealousy and enmity (vide Bhāgavata 3.29.7-10).
The Bhagavadgītā (7.16) offers a different classification: आर्त (one who is afflicted by serious problems, needing immediate succour), arthārthi (one desirous of worldly gains that cannot be easily obtained by human efforts), jijñāsu (the inquirer of Truth) and jñāni (the enlightened one). Each succeeding devotee is considered as superior to the preceding one.
The bhaktas may also be classified into different groups, depending upon the type of भक्ति they practise towards God. For instance, those who cultivate dāsya-भक्ति (devotion of the servant towards his master, like हनुमान्’s towards राम) form one group. Those that practise sakhya-भक्ति (an attitude of friendship, like अर्जुन’s or उद्धव’s towards कृष्ण) belong to another group. Others who practise vātsalyabhakti (maternal love towards the child, as यशोदा’s towards the child कृष्ण) fall into another group. Still others like आण्डाऌ and Mīrā, who practised madhurabhakti or conjugal love towards the Lord, form another group.
An ideal भक्त is one who has no hatred or enmity towards anyone. He is full of compassion and friendly feeling towards all. He is free from egoism and possessiveness. He is equanimous in plea-sure and pain, ever forgiving and ever contented. He has mastered his passions and dedicated his मिन्द् to God. He can never cause unrest in others nor can he be upset by others in anyway. He is beyond all dualities of the mundane life. He is therefore, extremely dear to the Lord (vide Bhagavadgītā 12.13-20).
See also BHAKTI and BHAKTIYOGA.
